messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Mateo Rodriguez, a thirty-five-year-old guitarist, arrived for the intake with the wary posture of someone who had trained himself never to stop moving. He had come to believe that stillness was dangerous—that the moment his hands were quiet and no one was speaking to him, the memory would surface in pieces he could not control. The accident had happened eighteen months ago, on a damp February night, while he was driving to a club in East LA. A pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan on the driver’s side. Mateo remembered the sound of metal crumpling, the windshield cracking, the paramedic’s voice asking him to squeeze a hand. But when he tried to recall the sequence in order, to tell the story start to finish, the memory would not cooperate. He could bring up only fragments—the taste of blood, the sensation of being pinned, the paramedic’s face—and they never seemed to fit together. It was as if the event had been broken into pieces and scattered, and he could not find all of them. This had troubled him deeply, because he felt he ought to be able to remember what had happened, ought to be able to make sense of it. Instead, he lived with the vague certainty that something important was missing.

In the months after the accident, Mateo had developed a relentless schedule. He lined up every night with a band or a session, then stayed out afterward with whoever would stay with him—bandmates, old friends, even strangers at the bar. He had become terrified of his own internal world. When he was alone, the fragments would push in without warning, and he would feel a wave of heat rising in his chest, a tightness in his jaw that frightened him. What scared him most was not the anger itself but the possibility that he would lose control of it—that he would say something brutal, or worse, act on it. He had always been a steady, easygoing man; now he felt like a live wire. The injustice of the accident had calcified inside him. The other driver had been arrested but released on bail, and the court date kept getting postponed. Nothing had been done. No one had apologized. The world had moved on as if what happened to Mateo meant nothing, and that sense of unfairness gnawed at him every day.

He avoided talking about the event with anyone, even his wife, Carla. When she asked how he was doing, he said “fine” and changed the subject. He did not want to think about it either—did not want to risk the memory surfacing, or the rage that might follow. He could not practice guitar alone at home anymore because the silence of the practice room invited the fragments. So he practiced with other musicians, always in company. He booked more gigs than he could comfortably handle, often playing four or five nights a week, sometimes double-shifts. The constant socialising kept the thoughts at bay, but it had cost him. Carla had started sleeping in the guest room; she told him she felt like a stranger in her own home, that he was never really there even when he was physically present. He had missed her birthday because he was at a jam session with a group he barely knew, and he had not even felt guilty about it at the time—he had only felt relief at not being alone.

Mateo’s life as a musician had once been his joy. Now it had become his shield. He took every opportunity to perform because performing meant being surrounded. But the music itself had lost its colour; he played mechanically, his mind elsewhere, watching for the gap between songs when the room would go quiet and he might hear his own thoughts. The accident had stolen something he could not name, and he was certain his life had been destroyed—not his body, which had healed, but something inside him. He no longer trusted himself to be alone. He no longer trusted himself not to explode. He came to therapy only because Carla had given him an ultimatum: get help, or she would leave. He sat in the chair with his hands clenched, ready to deflect, but a part of him was desperately hoping that someone might show him how to put the pieces back together.
